Interrogative means "relating to, expressing, or having the nature of a question."

Whenever something is described as interrogative, it means that thing is tied to the act of questioning — it either is a question, sounds like a question, or functions as part of a question.

Think of the word as a close cousin of "interrogate," which means to question someone intensely. An interrogative thing is simply something that questions, or belongs to the world of questioning.

The adjective "interrogative" appears in two broad areas: everyday language and grammar. Both flow from the same core idea — questioning.

1. In Everyday Language

Here, "interrogative" describes a tone, look, expression, or manner that feels like a question — even when no words are spoken.

Examples:

  • "She gave him an interrogative look."
    She looked at him in a way that clearly said, "What's going on?" Her expression itself was a silent question.
  • "He spoke in an interrogative tone."
    His voice had a rising, questioning quality — the kind you use when you're unsure or probing for an answer.
  • "The detective's interrogative manner made everyone nervous."
    The detective had a habit of constantly asking questions, examining things closely, and probing for information.

In these uses, you're saying that something carries the spirit or feeling of a question, even if it isn't a question in the grammatical sense.

2. In Grammar

This is where the word is most precisely and frequently used. In grammar, "interrogative" is used to label and describe the specific words, sentences, and structures that are used to ask questions.

Here are the key grammatical terms that use "interrogative" as an adjective:

a) Interrogative Sentence

An interrogative sentence is a sentence that asks a question. It is one of the four types of sentences (the others being declarative, imperative, and exclamatory).

  • "Are you coming to the party?" — interrogative sentence
  • "What time does the train leave?" — interrogative sentence
  • "I am coming to the party." — NOT interrogative (this is a statement)

The defining feature of an interrogative sentence is that it seeks information or a response. In English, these sentences often begin with a verb or a question word, and they typically end with a question mark.

b) Interrogative Pronouns

These are specific pronouns whose entire job is to ask questions. They stand in for an unknown person or thing that the speaker wants to identify.

The interrogative pronouns in English are: who, whom, whose, what, which.

  • "Who broke the window?"
  • "What are you thinking about?"
  • "Which of these bags is yours?"
  • "Whom did you speak to?"
  • "Whose car is parked outside?"

In each case, the pronoun is asking about something unknown. That is what makes them interrogative — they are the question-asking pronouns.

c) Interrogative Adverbs

These are adverbs used to ask questions about place, time, reason, or manner.

The interrogative adverbs in English are: where, when, why, how.

  • "Where are you going?" (asks about place)
  • "When will she arrive?" (asks about time)
  • "Why did he leave?" (asks about reason)
  • "How does this machine work?" (asks about manner)

They are "interrogative" because they open up a question and ask for specific information in return.

d) Interrogative Adjectives

Some of the same question words — which, what, whose — can also act as adjectives. When they do, they sit directly before a noun and ask a question about it. In this role, they are called interrogative adjectives.

  • "Which restaurant do you prefer?" (Here, "which" describes the noun "restaurant" and asks a question about it.)
  • "What colour is your car?" (Here, "what" describes the noun "colour.")
  • "Whose jacket is this?" (Here, "whose" describes the noun "jacket.")

The difference from interrogative pronouns is subtle but important: when the word replaces a noun, it's a pronoun. When it stands beside and describes a noun, it's an adjective.

Compare:

  • "What do you want?" → "What" replaces a noun = interrogative pronoun
  • "What colour do you want?" → "What" describes "colour" = interrogative adjective

e) Interrogative Clause

An interrogative clause is a group of words within a longer sentence that functions as a question or carries a questioning meaning.

  • "I asked whether she had eaten."
  • "Tell me what you know."
  • "I wonder why he left so suddenly."

The underlined parts are interrogative clauses — they express a question embedded inside a larger sentence.

If something is called interrogative, it means...
It asks a question, OR
It is used to form a question, OR
It has the quality or tone of a question

The word always circles back to one central idea: questioning.
A Simple Way to Remember It

Whenever you see or hear the word interrogative, just ask yourself: "Is this connected to asking a question?" If the answer is yes, the word fits perfectly. Whether it's a look on someone's face, a sentence structure, or a specific word like "who" or "where" — if it questions, it is interrogative.
